summary.text: Induction through the recurrence shows that both components at index $n$ are divisible by $2^{n-4}$, while finite residue checks propagated by periods $12$ modulo $5$ and $24$ modulo $7$ show that the first component is nonzero (indices $1\bmod 3$ are not divisible by $5$, and all others are not divisible by $7$). Hence for fixed $k\ge2$ and $n\ge k+4$, the nonzero first component contains at least $k$ factors of $2$, so its $k$-th prime factor is always $2$ and the sequence is eventually constant.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n,b_n)\) be the integer pair defined by
\[
(a_0,b_0)=(1,1),\qquad (a_1,b_1)=(2,1),
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+2}&=a_{n+1}b_n+a_nb_{n+1},\\
b_{n+2}&=a_{n+1}b_n-a_nb_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus A382590 is the sequence \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\).

For a nonzero integer \(x\), list the prime factors of \(|x|\), with multiplicity, in nondecreasing order. The \(k\)-th prime factor means the entry in position \(k\), with positions numbered starting at \(1\). If there are fewer than \(k\) entries, its value is defined to be \(1\); the same convention is used for \(x=0,\pm1\). We will prove something stronger than eventual periodicity: for each fixed \(k\ge2\), the \(k\)-th prime factor of \(a_n\) is equal to \(2\) for every \(n\ge k+4\).

The proof has three main parts. First, an increasing power of \(2\) divides both components of the recurrence. Second, a modular argument shows that no \(a_n\) is zero. Finally, these two facts force the first \(k\) prime factors of \(|a_n|\) to be \(2\).

## 1. Growing powers of two

We claim that for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
2^{\max(n-4,0)}\mid a_n
\quad\text{and}\quad
2^{\max(n-4,0)}\mid b_n.
\tag{1}
\]
Here and below the exponent \(n-4\), when regarded as a natural-number subtraction, means \(\max(n-4,0)\).

The initial pairs through index \(6\), obtained directly from the recurrence, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}
n&0&1&2&3&4&5&6\\ \hline
a_n&1&2&3&5&8&18&20\\
b_n&1&1&1&1&2&-2&52.
\end{array}
\]
For \(0\le n\le4\), the required power is \(2^0=1\). At \(n=5\), both \(18\) and \(-2\) are divisible by \(2=2^{5-4}\). At \(n=6\), both \(20\) and \(52\) are divisible by \(4=2^{6-4}\). Thus (1) holds for \(0\le n\le6\).

Now let \(n\ge7\), and suppose (1) is known at all smaller indices. In particular,
\[
2^{n-5}\mid a_{n-1},b_{n-1},
\qquad
2^{n-6}\mid a_{n-2},b_{n-2}.
\]
Consequently both products
\[
a_{n-1}b_{n-2}
\quad\text{and}\quad
a_{n-2}b_{n-1}
\]
are divisible by
\[
2^{(n-5)+(n-6)}=2^{2n-11}.
\]
Since \(n\ge7\), we have \(2n-11\ge n-4\), so both products are divisible by \(2^{n-4}\). Their sum and their difference are therefore also divisible by \(2^{n-4}\). By the defining recurrence, those sum and difference are respectively \(a_n\) and \(b_n\). This proves (1) by strong induction.

In particular,
\[
2^{n-4}\mid a_n\qquad(n\ge4).
\tag{2}
\]

It remains important to know that \(a_n\ne0\). Without this, divisibility by arbitrarily large powers of \(2\) would give no information about a finite prime-factor list. We establish nonvanishing using moduli \(5\) and \(7\).

## 2. Periodicity modulo 5

We first prove that, for every \(n\ge3\),
\[
(a_{n+12},b_{n+12})\equiv(a_n,b_n)\pmod5.
\tag{3}
\]
The two initial comparisons needed for the induction are obtained by iterating the recurrence modulo \(5\):
\[
(a_3,b_3)\equiv(0,1),\qquad (a_{15},b_{15})\equiv(0,1)\pmod5,
\]
and
\[
(a_4,b_4)\equiv(3,2),\qquad (a_{16},b_{16})\equiv(3,2)\pmod5.
\]
Thus (3) holds for \(n=3,4\).

For the induction step, take \(n\ge5\) and assume (3) at all smaller indices for which it is stated. In particular, it holds at \(n-1\) and \(n-2\). Using the recurrence,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+12}
 &=a_{n+11}b_{n+10}+a_{n+10}b_{n+11}\\
 &\equiv a_{n-1}b_{n-2}+a_{n-2}b_{n-1}
 =a_n\pmod5,
\end{aligned}
\]
and similarly
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+12}
 &=a_{n+11}b_{n+10}-a_{n+10}b_{n+11}\\
 &\equiv a_{n-1}b_{n-2}-a_{n-2}b_{n-1}
 =b_n\pmod5.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (3).

We now use (3) to prove
\[
n\equiv1\pmod3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 5\nmid a_n.
\tag{4}
\]
For the indices below \(15\) that are congruent to \(1\) modulo \(3\), direct recurrence computation gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
n&1&4&7&10&13\\ \hline
a_n\bmod5&2&3&1&2&4.
\end{array}
\]
All these residues are nonzero.

For \(n\ge15\) with \(n\equiv1\pmod3\), we may subtract \(12\). Since \(12\equiv0\pmod3\), the index \(n-12\) is again congruent to \(1\) modulo \(3\); moreover \(n-12\ge3\), so (3) applies and gives
\[
a_n\equiv a_{n-12}\pmod5.
\]
Repeatedly subtracting \(12\) eventually reaches one of the already checked indices \(1,4,7,10,13\), without changing the residue class of \(a_n\) modulo \(5\). Equivalently, this is a strong induction on \(n\). Since the terminal residue is nonzero, \(5\nmid a_n\), proving (4).

## 3. Periodicity modulo 7

We next prove that, for every \(n\ge7\),
\[
(a_{n+24},b_{n+24})\equiv(a_n,b_n)\pmod7.
\tag{5}
\]
The two initial comparisons, again found simply by applying the recurrence modulo \(7\), are
\[
(a_7,b_7)\equiv(0,4),\qquad (a_{31},b_{31})\equiv(0,4)\pmod7,
\]
and
\[
(a_8,b_8)\equiv(3,4),\qquad (a_{32},b_{32})\equiv(3,4)\pmod7.
\]
Thus (5) holds at \(n=7,8\).

For \(n\ge9\), assume (5) is known at the smaller indices \(n-1\) and \(n-2\). Exactly as above,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+24}
 &=a_{n+23}b_{n+22}+a_{n+22}b_{n+23}\\
 &\equiv a_{n-1}b_{n-2}+a_{n-2}b_{n-1}=a_n\pmod7,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+24}
 &=a_{n+23}b_{n+22}-a_{n+22}b_{n+23}\\
 &\equiv a_{n-1}b_{n-2}-a_{n-2}b_{n-1}=b_n\pmod7.
\end{aligned}
\]
This establishes (5) by induction.

We use this second periodicity to prove the complementary assertion
\[
n\not\equiv1\pmod3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 7\nmid a_n.
\tag{6}
\]
For all relevant indices below \(31\), recurrence computation modulo \(7\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrrrr}
n&0&2&3&5&6&8&9&11&12&14&15\\ \hline
a_n\bmod7&1&3&5&4&6&3&5&4&6&6&6
\end{array}
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrrr}
n&17&18&20&21&23&24&26&27&29&30\\ \hline
a_n\bmod7&2&3&6&5&1&3&3&3&2&6.
\end{array}
\]
These tables include precisely the integers \(0\le n<31\) with \(n\not\equiv1\pmod3\), and every displayed residue is nonzero.

Now suppose \(n\ge31\) and \(n\not\equiv1\pmod3\). Because \(24\equiv0\pmod3\), the smaller index \(n-24\) also is not congruent to \(1\) modulo \(3\). It is at least \(7\), so (5) gives
\[
a_n\equiv a_{n-24}\pmod7.
\]
Repeated subtraction of \(24\), or strong induction, reduces to one of the checked indices in the tables. Its residue modulo \(7\) is nonzero, and hence so is that of \(a_n\). This proves (6).

Every nonnegative integer \(n\) falls into exactly one of the two cases
\[
n\equiv1\pmod3
\quad\text{or}\quad
n\not\equiv1\pmod3.
\]
In the first case, (4) says that \(5\nmid a_n\); in the second, (6) says that \(7\nmid a_n\). Since every integer divides \(0\), either conclusion rules out \(a_n=0\). Therefore
\[
a_n\ne0\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0.
\tag{7}
\]

## 4. Consequence for the ordered prime factors

We need one elementary fact about prime factorizations.

**Lemma.** Let \(m\ne0\) be an integer, and let \(k\ge2\). If \(2^k\mid m\), then the \(k\)-th prime factor of \(m\), counted with multiplicity and ordered increasingly, is \(2\).

Indeed, \(2^k\mid m\) implies \(2^k\mid |m|\). In the prime factorization of the positive integer \(|m|\), the exponent of \(2\) is therefore at least \(k\). Thus the prime-factor list contains at least \(k\) occurrences of \(2\). Every prime is at least \(2\), and the list is in nondecreasing order. It follows that all of its first \(k\) entries are \(2\), so in particular its \(k\)-th entry is \(2\). Notice also that the list has length at least \(k\), so the fallback value \(1\) in the definition of the \(k\)-th prime factor does not arise. This proves the lemma.

For completeness, the ordering conclusion can also be seen directly: in any nondecreasing list all of whose entries are at least \(2\), if the list contains at least \(k\) copies of \(2\), no number larger than \(2\) can occur among the first \(k\) positions. If such a larger entry occurred there, every subsequent entry would also be larger than \(2\), leaving fewer than \(k\) copies of \(2\) in the entire list.

## 5. Eventual constancy and periodicity

Fix \(k>1\), so \(k\ge2\), and let \(n\ge k+4\). Then \(n-4\ge k\). By (2),
\[
2^{n-4}\mid a_n.
\]
Since \(k\le n-4\), we also have \(2^k\mid2^{n-4}\), and hence
\[
2^k\mid a_n.
\]
By (7), \(a_n\ne0\). The lemma therefore gives
\[
\text{the \(k\)-th prime factor of }a_n=2
\qquad(n\ge k+4).
\tag{8}
\]
Thus the sequence of \(k\)-th prime factors is not merely eventually periodic; it is constant from index \(N_0=k+4\) onward.

Explicitly, take period \(p=1\). For every \(n\ge N_0=k+4\), both \(n\) and \(n+1\) are at least \(k+4\), so (8) yields
\[
\operatorname{kpf}_k(a_{n+1})=2=\operatorname{kpf}_k(a_n).
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{kpf}_k(a_{n+p})=\operatorname{kpf}_k(a_n)
\qquad\text{for all }n\ge N_0,
\]
with the positive period \(p=1\). This proves the conjectured eventual periodicity for every integer \(k>1\).
